abstract: We present late-time photometry (~100-400 days after peak) and nebular-phase optical/NIR spectroscopy (100-360 days) of the Type Ia supernova (SN Ia) SN 2023bee. This SN Ia was observed TESS immediately before and after explosion and showed a relatively weak early excess light-curve feature detected in multiple UV and optical bands. Possible explanations for this early excess feature include interaction between the SN ejecta and a non-degenerate companion, or the decay of radioactive isotopes synthesized near the ejecta surface in a sub-$\text{M}_\text{Ch}$ double-detonation scenario. However, the degeneracies and incompleteness of existing models have so far prevented a definitive conclusion about its progenitor system. Nebular-phase spectra provide a complementary probe of SN Ia progenitors by constraining stripped H/He-rich material and iron-group abundances sensitive to the progenitor white dwarf density. We report the non-detection of narrow H/He features in nebular phase optical/NIR spectra of SN 2023bee, placing upper limits of $m^{\text{stripped}}_\text{H}\lesssim5.0\times10^{-3}\text{ M}_\odot$ and $m_\text{He}^{\text{stripped}}\lesssim1.2\times10^{-4}\text{ M}_\odot$. These limits strongly disfavor a non-degenerate companion and suggest that companion interaction is unlikely to explain the early excess of SN 2023bee. We also performed line-diagnostic measurements on the 7200 Åcomplex using multi-Gaussian fitting and continuum estimation, with the inferred velocities validated against NIR spectrum at the similar phase. The resulting low Ni-to-Fe mass ratio, $m_\text{Ni}/m_\text{Fe}\lesssim 0.06$, is broadly consistent with a sub-$M_{\text{Ch}}$ double-detonation progenitor system.
title: Constraints on the Progenitor of SN 2023bee from its Nebular-Phase Spectra

abstract: Historical astronomical plates provide a long temporal baseline for time-domain astrophysics, but degradation and structural artifacts can hinder automated astrometric calibration. We present Plate-YOLO, a framework that combines source detection and stellar classification in one detector and supplies source catalogs to a separate astrometric solver. The detector adapts YOLOv5 with Space-to-Depth feature rearrangement, SimAM attention, a high-resolution P2 head, and a Normalized Wasserstein Distance loss for small bounding boxes. A Gaia-guided fine-tuning procedure uses initially solved plates to construct labels for a new archive. On 150 UBAI plates for which the conventional pipeline had failed, the Chinese-trained model solved 40 plates, and target-archive fine-tuning recovered a further 106, giving an overall recovery rate of 146/150 (97.3%). In the reported hardware configuration, source extraction took 6.61 s per plate for Plate-YOLO and 16.73 s for SExtractor. These results demonstrate the practical value of adapting source detection to degraded historical plates.
comment: 14 pages, 6 figures, accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal
title: Plate-YOLO: An End-to-End Object Detection Framework for Robust Astrometric Registration of Historical Plates

abstract: Velocity-resolved reverberation mapping (RM) is one of the most powerful tools for probing the geometry and kinematics of the broad-line region in active galactic nuclei. However, its interpretation may be non-unique, as similar velocity-delay signatures can arise from different combinations of BLR geometry and kinematics. To address this degeneracy, this series of studies develops velocity-resolved ionization mapping (IM) as a complementary technique. In this second paper of the series, we construct photoionization-based BLR models to quantitatively demonstrate the diagnostic power of the joint RM+IM framework. We calculate local \ha\ and \hb\ emissivities with Cloudy, couple them with disk-like BLR models, and generate synthetic velocity-dependent line fluxes, lags, and Balmer decrements. The model reproduces the observed anti-correlation between the integrated BD and the incident ionizing continuum, with scatter naturally introduced by reverberation delays. We show that a virialized elliptical BLR can produce diverse velocity-delay maps and velocity-resolved lags that mimic RM signatures commonly attributed to virialized motion, inflow, or outflow. In contrast, the velocity-resolved BD is sensitive to the symmetry of the BLR gas distribution, providing a key diagnostic for distinguishing eccentric geometry from non-virial motions. Through proof-of-concept comparisons with one double-peaked and one single-peaked AGN, we show that an elliptical-disk BLR can simultaneously reproduce the observed line profiles, velocity-resolved lags, and velocity-resolved BDs. These results provide a quantitative basis for IM, support the presence of eccentric BLR structures in AGNs, and demonstrate the potential of joint RM+IM analyses to break the BLR geometry-kinematics degeneracy.
title: Velocity-resolved Ionization Mapping of the Broad-line Region. II. Signatures of Eccentric Broad-line Regions from a Quantitative Photoionization-Based Model

abstract: We present the DARWIN project, a suite of cosmological simulations with RAMSES to study dwarf-galaxy formation and evolution across diverse environments. DARWIN-1 is a full-box simulation in a cubic volume of $(65.5\,{\rm cMpc})^3$ with a minimum cell size of 500pc, while DARWIN-2 comprises zoom-in simulations of 24 field regions and a Milky Way analog connected to a filament, reaching 62.5pc resolution. The simulations employ baryonic physics tailored to their aims. For DARWIN-2, we include radiative transfer in three photon energy bands to trace hydrogen and helium ionization. DARWIN-1 reproduces the cosmic star formation rate density and galaxy stellar mass functions reasonably well at $z>1$. Both simulations broadly reproduce observed stellar mass-halo mass relations, chemical abundances, star-formation surface densities, and black hole-galaxy scaling relations. At lower redshift, DARWIN-1 shows an excess in the number density of massive galaxies, although the inferred stellar content of massive halos depends on the definition of galaxy stellar mass. Other systematic differences arise from spatial resolution, feedback efficiency, and environmental selection. To facilitate comparison with observations, we generate mock images using the radiative transfer codes SKIRT and Powderday. We also explore a machine-learning approach to mitigate resolution-driven biases in the dwarf galaxy properties of DARWIN-1 using the higher-resolution DARWIN-2 simulations. The DARWIN simulation suite therefore provides a comprehensive numerical framework for studying the formation, evolution, and internal physics of dwarf galaxies in a cosmological context.
comment: 33 pages, 18 figures, submitted to ApJ, any comments welcome
title: The DARWIN Project: Cosmological Simulations of Galaxy Formation down to Dwarf Scales in Diverse Environments

abstract: We use the Cross-Tracer Clustering Ratio (CTCR) acoustic response estimator, a new probe of morphology-dependent galaxy clustering in photometric surveys. CTCR is the ratio of the auto-power spectrum of early-type galaxies (ETGs) to their cross-power spectrum with late-type galaxies (LTGs). In the matched-kernel deterministic linear-bias limit the CTCR cancels the complete projected matter spectrum, including the baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) wiggles, leaving only the relative linear bias. This makes the ratio uniquely sensitive to physics beyond deterministic linear bias: any residual acoustic structure in the CTCR must arise from a difference between the normalised non-linear responses of the two tracers. We, for the first time, exploit this property to model the measured ratio as a smooth scale-dependent baseline multiplied by a scale-dependent acoustic template, and constrain the amplitude $A_{\rm morph}$ of the differential acoustic response jointly with the BAO dilation parameter $α$. Applying the estimator to nine bins of the DESI Legacy Survey Data Release 8 spanning $0.1 < z < 0.9$, we obtain$α= 0.9997 \pm 0.0383$, consistent with the Planck 2018 $Λ$CDM prediction, and $A_{\rm morph} = 0.369 \pm 0.307$, consistent with zero. A Bayesian model comparison yields at most a 2.6$σ$ preference for the acoustic template over a smooth-only baseline. The estimator is model-independent, requires no external calibration of the absolute bias, and is directly applicable to the wide-field imaging surveys that will define the next decade of cosmology. It offers a new route to testing halo occupation and assembly-bias models, and an independent, systematics-robust cross-check of BAO measurements from spectroscopic surveys.
title: A Morphology-Based Cross-Tracer Ratio for Robust BAO Tests

abstract: Gravitational-wave dark sirens can be combined with galaxy catalogues to provide a measurement of the Hubble constant. This inference requires assigning each potential host galaxy a probability of hosting a merger, but the appropriate weighting is uncertain because the binary merger rate may trace different galaxy properties, such as stellar mass or star formation rate, depending on the underlying formation channel. We introduce a flexible framework in which the dark-siren population is described as a mixture of two host-weighting prescriptions, with the mixing fraction inferred jointly with $H_0$. These components may be interpreted as subpopulations associated with distinct binary-formation environments. Using simulated catalogues, we show that marginalising over uncertainty in the host-population mixture preserves unbiased constraints on $H_0$, while allowing the gravitational-wave data to constrain the relative contribution of the two host populations. In particular, an A#-like detector network with $\mathcal{O}(10^3)$ dark sirens may be able to exclude scenarios in which the host population traces only one of the two weighting prescriptions. Dark-siren analyses may therefore provide robust cosmological measurements and new information about how merging compact binaries trace the galaxy population.
title: Hostbusters: constraining $H_0$ and binary formation channels through gravitational-wave host galaxy associations

abstract: While known interstellar scattering screens are largely confined to the Galactic disk, the scattering properties of the circumgalactic medium (CGM) in the deep Galactic halo have remained unexplored. Using observations from the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we report the first detection of scintillation arcs in the secondary spectra of the high-latitude pulsar J1312+1810A (M53A). Under the 1D anisotropic and 2D isotropic thin-screen models considered here, the inferred scintillation screen distances are $12.8_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.7_{-3.5}^{+2.8}$\,kpc, respectively. These model-dependent estimates correspond to Galactic heights of $12.6_{-3.5}^{+2.6}$ and $11.5_{-3.5}^{+2.7}$\,kpc, placing the candidate screen among the highest-altitude scattering structures inferred to date. The strong, time-variable scintillation asymmetry suggests substantial electron-density inhomogeneity within the screen. We speculate that this screen is associated with small-scale structures near the shock boundary of the northern eROSITA bubble. These results support the presence of discrete, inhomogeneous scattering structures deep within the Galactic halo, far beyond the regions where localized stellar feedback is typically concentrated, and highlight pulsar scintillation as a promising probe of small-scale ionized structures in the CGM.
title: A high-Galactic-altitude scattering screen: scintillation from Globular Cluster pulsar M53A

abstract: Gravitational-wave standard sirens provide a calibration-free measure of distances, offering important input on the long-standing tension between early- and late-Universe measurements of the Hubble constant ($H_0$). In the absence of an electromagnetic counterpart, the dark siren method can be employed to statistically correlate a gravitational wave event's localization with a galaxy catalog of potential hosts. We present a measurement of the Hubble constant using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey Data Release 3 and the fifth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog. Applying the dark siren method to a large, photometrically heterogeneous footprint required revised catalog-construction choices: a faint apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r<20$) to control known photometric-redshift bias, a bright apparent-magnitude threshold ($m_r>15.5$) to exclude saturated sources, implementation of an evolving luminosity function parameterization, and de-biasing survey regions based on survey depth and photometric redshift precision. With these choices applied to DELVE, we obtain $H_0= 67.4^{+13.0}_{-11.2}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ from dark sirens alone, and $H_0= 70.6^{+8.7}_{-7.0}\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ when combined with the bright siren GW170817. We test other galaxy catalog configuration choices, and find subdominant influence from photometric band choice and luminosity function parameterization on the final $H_0$ posterior. Our results demonstrate that extending the dark siren method to wider-area, non-uniform galaxy surveys is feasible and provides additional constraining power on $H_0$ relative to the spectral siren method, opening the door for analyses with forthcoming galaxy catalogs from LSST, Euclid, and Roman.
comment: 9 Pages, 6 Figures, 2 Tables, Submitted to A&A
title: Constraints on the Cosmic Expansion Rate Using the DECam Local Volume Exploration Survey and the Fifth Gravitational Wave Transient Catalog

abstract: Coeval stellar populations offer a unique advantage for studying stellar physics because their members share a common age and broadly similar initial chemical composition, allowing the free parameters in stellar models to be constrained more efficiently. Meanwhile, asteroseismology, through the study of pulsation modes that propagate through stellar interiors, provides powerful constraints on internal structure and the physical processes operating beneath stellar atmospheres. The combination of coeval-population studies and asteroseismology therefore provides an unparalleled laboratory for testing and improving stellar evolutionary and structural models. Using light curves from the Kepler and TESS space missions, together with membership constraints based on Gaia astrometry, we identify g-mode period-spacing patterns in dozens of early-type ($T_{\rm eff} \gtrsim 7000\,\mathrm{K}$) main-sequence stars across 16 stellar groups. From these patterns, we infer near-core rotation rates $f_\mathrm{rot}$ and measure the asymptotic spacing $Π_0$ of g modes, tracing both angular-momentum transport and the evolution of the convective stellar cores. Using our homogeneous set of g-mode stellar-group members spanning a wide range of ages, we show that near-core rotation in early-type stars decreases with stellar evolution. We compare our results with existing model predictions. Our $Π_0$ measurements still show discrepancies with current stellar models for reasons that remain unclear, as reported in several previous studies. We also report two g-mode pre-main-sequence pulsators and three pulsating blue stragglers. Our sample provides a useful basis for calibrating stellar models in future ensemble asteroseismic studies of coeval stellar populations.
comment: 26 pages, 16 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJS
title: Gravity-mode main-sequence asteroseismology of 16 open clusters and associations

abstract: Following recent observations of unexpectedly massive galaxies at high redshift by the James Webb Space Telescope, the revision of Dark Matter (DM) models --specifically regarding how DM couples to gravity-- has become a central topic in Cosmology. In this paper, we develop an axion model for Cold Dark Matter (CDM) with a non-minimal coupling to gravity. From this framework, we evaluate the gravitational instability in the hydrodynamic limit. Our results demonstrate how gravitational instabilities depend on the non-minimal coupling parameter, providing a novel tool for aligning with the high-redshift observations from the James Webb Space Telescope.
title: Gravitational Instability of Cold Axion Dark Matter Beyond Minimal Coupling

abstract: PDS~70, the only system with two directly imaged protoplanets embedded in their natal disk, is a benchmark for giant-planet formation theory. Interpreting the planetary luminosities requires a precise age for the host star, but the widely adopted isochronal age of $5.4\pm1.0$~Myr is substantially younger than ages inferred for the Upper Centaurus--Lupus (UCL) population with which it is associated. We address this discrepancy by determining a new kinematic age for PDS~70 using radial velocities for 405 candidate members of the Scorpius--Centaurus T subcomponent from the Wide Field Spectrograph (WiFeS) on the ANU 2.3~m telescope, reducing uncertainties by a factor of $\sim5.5$ compared to \textit{Gaia}. %We supplement these measurements with H$α$ and lithium equivalent widths as youth diagnostics. We combine these with \textit{Gaia} DR3 astrometry in the \texttt{Chronostar} kinematic reconstruction framework to derive a posterior-weighted kinematic age of approximately $10$--$15$~Myr for all the T subcomponent stars, with a kinematic age of $\approx 12$--$16$~Myr for PDS 70, ruling out ages as young as the published isochronal estimate. At this kinematic age, PDS~70~\textit{b}'s (and to a lesser extent, PDS~70~\textit{c}'s) luminosity is incompatible with warm-start cooling tracks under current dynamical mass constraints. The most natural interpretation is that PDS~70~\textit{b} formed $\approx10.5$ Myr after its host star, and no less than $\approx7.7$ Myr after it.
comment: 25 pages, 25 figures, submitted to MNRAS. Comments are welcome! Related data (and near future: related code) can be accessed at https://github.com/aruuniima/T-subcomponent_PDS70 and the Chronostar code is publicly available at https://github.com/tcrundall/chronostar-tng
title: Kinematic structure and age of a Scorpius--Centaurus subcomponent: implications for PDS 70 planetary system

abstract: In this note, we introduce the Hubble susceptibility of cosmological-collider masses, encoded in the scale dependence of the squeezed-limit oscillation. Heavy fields generically receive Hubble-induced mass corrections during inflation, and we show that the local oscillation frequency and its drift can disentangle such corrections from an intrinsic mass contribution at leading slow-roll and adiabatic order.
title: Hubble Susceptibility: Beyond Effective-Mass Spectroscopy in the Cosmological Collider

abstract: Light curves reveal stellar variability and support studies of stellar evolution and cosmic distances. Reliable classification is therefore important for large time-domain surveys. We present HyQ-LC for ten-class stellar light-curve classification using 359 handcrafted features and 633,034 training objects. The main model combines a window multilayer perceptron (MLP) backbone with a nine-qubit readout using amplitude encoding and angle re-uploading. Both this hybrid and its pure-MLP control have 44,238 parameters. On a shared 20,000-object test set, the hybrid has macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) point gains of 0.8276 and 1.2393 percentage points over the pure MLP on two fine-tuning seeds. A separate fixed-fusion configuration achieves slightly higher Macro-F1 but lower accuracy than approximately budget-matched LightGBM. Its positive class-level differences are concentrated in CEP, RRC, and ROT, while the full-budget LightGBM reference scores higher on both metrics. All circuits are simulated classically. The comparisons retain existing validation-selected checkpoints and use the same test objects, with features, predictions, and recomputation code publicly available. The results identify point-estimate improvements over the tested controls while leaving the specific contribution of the quantum branch unresolved.
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/bestdo77/quantum-lightcurve-hybrid
title: HyQ-LC: Improving Light-Curve Classification with Hybrid Quantum--Classical Learning

abstract: During its orbit around the Milky Way, the Solar System crosses different environments, including dense ISM regions. These encounters increase dust influx, leave geological signatures, and affect the heliosphere. For the local ISM, we estimate crossing frequencies and durations, the fraction of time spent above gas density thresholds, and how Solar vertical motion and ISM stratification influence these statistics. We quantify gas influx and dust exposure. We use Gaia-based 3D dust maps of the Solar neighborhood, sampled by integrating the Solar System along its Galactic orbit while rigidly translating the maps. From the resulting density time series, encounter statistics and fluxes are derived. We find that the Solar System spends most of its time in low density environments, while crossings of dense gas become rarer with increasing density threshold. For nH>=1cm^-3, the crossing frequency is above 600Gyr^-1, whereas thresholds around 200cm^-3 are crossed once per Gyr. Individual crossings last tens of kyr and become shorter at higher density thresholds. The inferred durations soon become nearly constant, reflecting the finite spatial resolution of the maps. The Sun spends 18 to 47% of the sampled time above 1cm^-3, and 1 to 10% above 10cm^-3. The residence fraction can be reproduced by combining the vertical volume filling factor of gas with the fraction of time spent by the Sun at each height. Within the current vertical range sampled by the Sun, we find no clear enhancement of crossing statistics during midplane passages, suggesting that these do not necessarily lead to periodic perturbations of the Solar System. About 50% of the gas influx is contributed by gas with nH<=3-4cm^-3, and about 90% by gas with nH<=48cm^-3. Our results provide a first order, data driven estimate of ISM encounter statistics, gas influx, and dust exposure along the Solar System's Galactic orbit.
title: The Solar System through dust maps. Encounter statistics with interstellar gas

abstract: Gravitational lensing can split the signal of a binary merger into two images, which either overlap and interfere or arrive as separate events. We show that the matched-filter output of every two-image template can be straightforwardly constructed from the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) time series that searches already compute with unlensed templates. This enables a marginalized detection statistic that increases search sensitivity without additional matched filtering and is more than 150 times faster than an explicit lensed template bank. For overlapping images in the geometric-optics regime, our two-image method recovers $\gtrsim97\%$ of the optimal SNR from point-mass and singular isothermal lenses, compared with as little as $67\%$ captured by unlensed templates, with substantial gains also for Chang-Refsdal and cored isothermal lenses. Overlapping lensed signals moreover fail the signal-consistency test that is used to down-rank noise transients. Our two-image method restores the consistency and increases the sensitive volume by roughly $2$-$4\times$ for the strongly down-ranked signals. For separated images, our method enables an efficient coherent search for pairs in which neither image is significant alone. Near fold caustics, this increases the sensitive volume by factors of 1.8-2.6 over requiring two independent detections, and up to 1.6 over a targeted counterpart search. Our method is applicable to any matched-filtering search.
comment: 7+11 pages, 3+5 figures. The codes associated with this paper are publicly available, together with the data and scripts needed to reproduce all of its figures https://github.com/JayWadekar/lensed-gw-unlensed-templates
title: Searching for lensed gravitational waves with unlensed templates

abstract: We revisit a late-time, model-independent distance-consistency framework that combines strong gravitational lensing systems (SGLS), ultraviolet/X-ray quasars (QSOs), and 38 Sunyaev--Zel'dovich/X-ray galaxy-cluster angular-diameter distances. The analysis focuses on systematics rather than on presenting a competitive curvature measurement. Starting from the 158-system SGLS catalog, we exclude 30 systems that violate the lensing-geometric requirement $D_{A,ls}/D_{A,s}<1$ in the isothermal reference case $γ_{\rm lens}=2$, leaving a fixed 128-system SGLS parent sample for cross-matching with 1598 QSOs. A deterministic maximum-cardinality, minimum-mismatch one-to-one assignment yields 100 SGLS--QSO pairs at the nominal $Δd/d=5\%$ threshold. We propagate the measured X-ray flux uncertainties and the intrinsic QSO scatter, and, crucially, we include the full $38\times38$ covariance induced by using the same QSO distances in the kernel-smoothed cluster predictions. With $Ω_K\sim\mathcal{U}[-10,10]$, the joint posterior is $Ω_K=2.085^{+1.634}_{-1.103}$ (68\%; central 95\% interval $[0.269,6.028]$). We do not interpret the positive shift as evidence for an open Universe. \added{This positive posterior offset is driven by cross-probe calibration tensions, sample-assignment effects, and the cluster anchor; it cannot be attributed to the intrinsic spatial geometry of the Universe.} The SGLS+QSO data alone leave curvature essentially prior dominated, $Ω_K=0.70^{+6.33}_{-7.12}$, whereas removing only the off-diagonal cluster covariance moves the posterior to $Ω_K=5.21^{+2.46}_{-2.07}$. Thus the cluster anchor supplies most of the curvature constraining power and its covariance materially changes the posterior location.
comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, Accepted for publication in Research in Astronomy and Astrophysics (RAA)
title: Late-time distance consistency and model-independent curvature inference with strong lensing, quasars, and galaxy clusters

abstract: Dust mass (M$_{Dust}$) is one of the key physical properties of galaxies that track the cold interstellar medium. However, the M$_{Dust}$ in merging galaxies is poorly understood. We aim to derive how the cold dust mass of galaxies is affected by major mergers at low redshifts. M$_{Dust}$ was estimated for approximately 500 major mergers in the North Ecliptic Pole extragalactic field using spectral energy distribution fitting runs with CIGALE, with different dust attenuation and emission models. We also analysed over 12 000 mergers from the SIMBA simulation using its M$_{Dust}$. We matched merging and non-merging systems in stellar mass, redshift, and local density, to enable a comparison of M$_{Dust}$. We then performed a second comparison using a control sample also matched in SFR. AGN host galaxies were then removed, and this matching repeated. Observed mergers have larger M$_{Dust}$ than the non-mergers by up to a factor of 1.82$\pm$0.35, or 1.60$\pm$0.44 without AGN-hosts. When matched by SFR, observed mergers show no significant change in M$_{Dust}$, both when including and excluding AGN-hosts. SIMBA galaxies show similar trends when AGN-hosts are included but there is still an increase in M$_{Dust}$ when matched by SFR. When AGN-hosts are excluded, the SIMBA mergers show smaller M$_{Dust}$ by a factor of 0.98$\pm$0.03, or 0.97$\pm$0.02 when matched in SFR. The higher the mass of a merger, the greater M$_{Dust}$ increase for observations for two of the CIGALE runs, or the smaller the decrease for SIMBA. Observed mergers are typically more dusty than their non-merging counterparts but only because they typically have higher SFRs, regardless of whether they host AGN or not. SIMBA mergers follow observations when AGN hosts are included, but show reduced M$_{Dust}$ when AGN hosts are removed. M$_{Dust}$ in SIMBA is linked to AGN in a way not seen in observations.
comment: 17 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables, 3 appendices, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
title: Effect of galaxy mergers on dust masses

abstract: We investigate the impact of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in the gravitational collapse of isolated low-mass cloud cores using three-dimensional non-ideal magnetohydrodynamics simulations. In the models explored in this study, we find that unipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with the super-Alfvénic turbulence of $M_{\rm{A}}>1$, where $M_{\rm{A}}$ is the Alfvén Mach number of the initial cloud core. In contrast, bipolar outflows are formed in cloud cores with $M_{\rm{A}}\lesssim1$. Our results suggest that the relative strength of the turbulence to the magnetic field in the initial cloud core plays a key role in the formation of unipolar outflows. We also find that no outflow is formed in cloud cores with the strong magnetic field of the dimensionless mass-to-flux ratio $μ=2$. The outflow morphologies can be used as tracers to indirectly estimate the relative strengths of the turbulence and magnetic field of the parent cloud cores.
title: Competitive roles of turbulence and magnetic field on the formation of unipolar outflows in isolated molecular cloud cores

abstract: We present the first local simulations of accretion disc breaking (or disc tearing) with differential precession. Precession can occur due to a non-spherical potential (e.g. tilted circumbinary discs), or relativistic effects (e.g. tilted discs around spinning black holes). This tends to induce a twist in the disc, potentially causing it to break into rings. We extend earlier work on free (unforced) warps in Held+2026 [arXiv:2511.18655v1] to include differential precession in the shearing box, and carry out quasi-2D, isothermal, high-resolution ($N = 32$ cells per scale-height $H$) numerical simulations in which an imposed precession drives a warp in a tilted disc in either the wavelike ($α< H/r$) or diffusive ($α> H/r$) regime. Our key finding is that, at sufficiently large tilts and precession amplitudes, the disc breaks into multiple (4-5) mutually tilted rings exhibiting a rich morphology: from wide ($\sim 10H$), flat rings to compact tori of width $\sim H$. Interactions between rings occur as a result of oblique shocks that form in the gaps between them, leading to instances of disc rejoining. Smaller tilts and precession amplitudes lead instead to parametric instability of inertial waves in the disc. We develop a linear viscous theory of bending waves under the influence of an imposed precession. Finally, we present a systematic study of the effects of grid-based dissipation on tilted discs, and find that numerical dissipation damps the tilt and induces precession. This effect decreases with resolution as $\propto (1/N)^β$, $2.3 \lesssim β\lesssim 3.9$.
title: Disc breaking and parametric instability in warped accretion discs driven by differential precession

abstract: Coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are major drivers of space weather, yet their thermodynamic evolution remains insufficiently constrained. This thesis develops a comprehensive framework linking CME kinematics, thermodynamics, internal force balance, and geoeffectiveness through analytical modelling and multi-viewpoint observations. The developed FRIS model uses observed kinematics to infer otherwise inaccessible internal plasma properties, including the polytropic index. A systematic investigation of fast CMEs reveals an initial heat-release phase followed by a transition towards near-isothermal evolution, typically around 3-9 solar radii. The evolving contributions of thermal-pressure and centrifugal forces, opposed by the Lorentz force, establish a connection between expansion and thermal evolution. The findings demonstrate the limitations of assuming a fixed polytropic index in magnetohydrodynamic models of CME propagation. At 1 au, in situ observations reveal persistent non-adiabatic evolution, accompanied by turbulence and localised intermittency. The interacting CMEs associated with the May 2024 great storm show restructured magnetic and thermal configurations, producing double-flux-rope-like signatures and species-dependent heating, with electron thermodynamics as a better indicator of recent interactions. Statistical analysis of nearly 600 ME demonstrates that 45% exhibit net heating with a solar cycle dependence. Notably, High-impact ejecta preferentially exhibit stronger heating signatures, establishing thermal state as a complementary diagnostic of geoeffectiveness. Overall, this thesis establishes CMEs as intrinsically non-adiabatic systems whose thermodynamic evolution is coupled to expansion, internal force balance, solar-cycle variability, and CME-CME interactions, with important implications for understanding geoeffectiveness and improving space-weather assessment.
comment: PhD Thesis, Indian Institute of Astrophysics & Pondicherry University, 271 pages, Contributing papers have been published independently in ApJ, A&A, MNRAS and JAA journals
title: Kinematics and Thermodynamics of Coronal Mass Ejections

abstract: High-Dynamic-Range (HDR) multi-band linear polarimetry of the solar corona during total solar eclipses provides a vital ground-based diagnostic tool for mapping plasma morphology and magnetic topology in the inner and middle corona. Extracting reliable polarimetric signals requires rigorous observational calibration, spatial co-alignment, and noise reduction via stacking. We report optical linear polarimetric observations acquired during the 8 April 2024 total solar eclipse from Dallas, Texas, USA, near solar maximum. Using a full-frame color CMOS detector paired with an 80~mm refractor, multi-band Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) images were recorded simultaneously across three polarizer orientations ($-60^\circ$, $0^\circ$, and $+60^\circ$) using a 9-step exposure bracket ($1/800\text{~s}$ to $1/3\text{~s}$). We present an end-to-end data-reduction pipeline incorporating: (i)~a novel astrometric registration framework that reconstructs Sun-centric solar-disk coordinates via lunar-limb fitting, catalog star plate-solving, and ephemeris displacement calculations, achieving sub-pixel alignment; (ii)~a photometrically linear exposure-normalization HDR image synthesis; and (iii)~Multi-scale Gaussian Normalization (MGN) coupled with Polarization-to-RGB chromatic mapping. The resulting structurally enhanced polarization composites unravel a complex solar-maximum coronal topology characterized by helmet streamers and fine-scale striations traceable out to $\sim3\,R_\odot$. This framework establishes a high-resolution, photometrically calibrated dataset ready for subsequent polarized brightness ($pB$) and electron density inversions.
comment: 23 pages, 8 figures. Accepted in Solar Physics
title: Linear Polarimetry of the Solar Corona during the Total Solar Eclipse of 8 April 2024: Multi-Band Observations and HDR Imaging

abstract: Cosmic filaments connect the nodes of the large-scale web and are thought to harbour a substantial fraction of the low-z baryon budget, yet a physically motivated framework for organising their diverse gas properties has been lacking. Here we show that the linear mass density $Λ$ = M_gas/L_fil, measured within the entropy radius r_K (the peak of the radial gas entropy profile) plays this role, analogous to mass in halo physics. Using TNG300-1 at z=0, we characterise the structural, thermodynamic, and chemical properties of 5637 filaments spanning more than two decades in $Λ$. Filaments form a continuous thermodynamic sequence with $Λ$, ranging from long, thin, cool, metal-poor structures to shorter, wider, hotter, and more enriched ones, with core temperatures spanning two orders of magnitude across the full WHIM window. The ratio of mass- to volume-weighted temperature reveals a shift in heat distribution: low-$Λ$ filaments have their hotter gas preferentially associated with denser material, whereas in high-$Λ$ filaments the hotter gas is diffuse. Well-defined scaling relations connect $Λ$ to temperature, electron density, pressure, entropy, and metallicity, with the T-$Λ$ scaling qualitatively consistent with gravitational heating. We present the first measurement of the gaseous linear mass density function, revealing a broad distribution with a flat low-$Λ$ regime and a steep exponential decline at high $Λ$, analogous to the halo mass function. The integrated Compton-y parameter $Y^{\rm int}$ scales systematically with $Λ$, providing a tSZ proxy accessible to current surveys. Finally, galaxy richness per unit length correlates tightly with $Λ$ (Pearson r=0.80), enabling $Λ$-based classification of filaments from spectroscopic surveys alone and guiding targeted searches for the missing baryons in the cosmic web.
title: Linear gas mass density: a unifying descriptor of Cosmic Filaments

abstract: The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of our Galaxy is a prime laboratory for interstellar chemistry because of its extreme conditions, such as shocks and high cosmic-ray ionisation rates. It is an efficient factory of molecules, with many species first discovered in CMZ sources. This document reviews key results from the study of the CMZ G+0.693-0.027 molecular cloud. Using ultra-sensitive broadband spectral surveys together with laboratory spectroscopy, more than 140 molecules have been identified, including 28 detected for the first time in the interstellar medium (ISM). These discoveries include prebiotic precursors of biomolecules, increasingly complex members of known molecular families, molecules containing periodic third-row elements (S, P, Na, Mg), high-energy stereo- and structural isomers, and new cations. Overall, these findings extend the known limits of interstellar chemical complexity and highlight the CMZ's potential to provide the molecular ingredients for prebiotic chemistry.

title: The Central Molecular Zone of our Galaxy, a chemical complexity factory: first interstellar detections of molecules towards G+0.693

abstract: Stars born in the high-$α$ disk can later acquire low angular momentum through dynamical scattering during early merger events. Their age--metallicity distribution thus provides a fossil record of the history of both star formation and dynamical perturbations in the early Milky Way disk. Here we identify a sample of 2,078 such stars from more than two million Gaia DR3 subgiants with robust determinations of ages, kinematics, and abundances. From this sample we reconstruct their intrinsic age--metallicity distribution with a forward modeling approach. Our results confirm that these scattered stars are older and more metal-poor than the bulk of the high-$α$ disk on average. In particular, the joint age--metallicity distribution reveals a robust two-component feature: a broad, dominant component with a peak age of $\sim$11.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.59$, and an older and more metal-poor component with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr and ${\rm [Fe/H]}\simeq-0.86$. The presence of this two-component structure suggests that the high-$α$ disk experienced episodic phases of star formation and chemical enrichment. The age distribution of the younger Splash component, compared with that of the high-$α$ disk, provides evidence for a substantial dynamical perturbation at a lookback time of 10.8--11.5~Gyr, possibly associated with an early passage of Gaia--Sausage--Enceladus (GSE). The older Splash component, with a peak age of $\sim$12.5~Gyr, may preserve signatures of an earlier interaction, possibly associated with the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles (LKH) event.
title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. I. Evidence from Low-angular-momentum, High-$α$ Stars Scattered Out of the Protodisk by Merger Events

abstract: Dwarf galaxies serve as fossils for understanding the early star formation history of the local Universe. In this work, we use stellar abundances for individual stars derived from the first data release of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI DR1) to investigate the star formation history of the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Draco. We simultaneously fit the stellar metallicity distribution function (MDF) and the [Mg/Fe]-[Fe/H] trend using the galactic chemical evolution (GCE) model flexCE. Our best-fit models imply a low star formation efficiency (SFE) of $0.003$ to $0.007\,\mathrm{Gyr}^{-1}$, which is about ten times lower than values reported in the literature, but consistent with recent SFE estimates for ultra-faint dwarf galaxies. By combining recent literature measurements, we find that the SFEs of Milky Way dwarf galaxies scale with stellar mass as $\mathrm{SFE}\propto M_\star^{0.24}$. A low star formation efficiency is associated with a strong outflow efficiency; we estimate a large wind mass-loading factor $η_{\mathrm{wind}}$ of approximately 172-260. This is well in line with the observed outflow-stellar mass relation and with the Feedback in Realistic Environment (FIRE) cosmological simulations. Our results demonstrate the power of large-scale, low-to-medium resolution stellar spectroscopic surveys to deliver robust constraints on the early formation history of galaxies in the local Universe.
comment: 19 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
title: Star formation history of Draco revealed by DESI DR1: suppressed early star formation efficiency for Milky Way dwarf galaxies

abstract: The nearby radio galaxy M87 is an ideal laboratory for studying accretion flows and relativistic jet emission. The EHT collaboration conducted the most comprehensive multi-wavelength observational campaign of M87, in which radio instruments with resolutions ranging from tens of microarcseconds to about an arcsecond sampled different portions of the outflow. We model these data using a radiatively inefficient accretion flow (RIAF) with winds and a new multi-zone jet model, initially magnetically dominated, in which we solve the transport equation for the non-thermal electrons as they are injected, advected, and cooled along the jet. We then compare each radio flux with the jet emission within an effective aperture set by the angular scale of the corresponding observation. The comparison across spatial scales favours a scenario in which the RIAF, rather than the jet, produces the compact $230~{\rm GHz}$ emission, while the jet dominates the lower-frequency radio, optical/UV and X-ray emission, but cannot produce the observed $γ$-rays. The RIAF connects the Bondi-scale gas supply to an accretion rate at the horizon of $1.1\times 10^{-5}$ of the Eddington rate, consistent with EHT polarimetry, and the two jets carry about a quarter of the accretion power, $1.2\times10^{43}~{\rm erg~s}^{-1}$ each. The framework presented in this work provides a simple way to disentangle the accretion-flow and jet contributions to the emission from nearby radio galaxies.
title: The accretion flow and jet of M87: broadband modelling across spatial scales

abstract: This thesis investigates the cosmological dynamics of primordial black holes (PBHs) within the Randall--Sundrum Type II braneworld scenario. The work comprises a preliminary discussion on gravitational collapse in the small-black-hole limit at early cosmological epochs, and two principal studies. The first study presents a fully relativistic treatment of PBH accretion in the early Universe, employing Michel accretion theory within the covariant Shiromizu--Maeda--Sasaki formalism. The analysis reveals that higher-dimensional effects substantially enhance early-time accretion onto light PBHs, with discrepancies between our black hole masses and previous estimates growing with cosmic time as $t^{0.33}$ --- a difference that reaches several orders of magnitude by the end of the strong-accretion epoch. This finding fundamentally alters the mapping between the initial PBH mass spectrum and present-day populations. The second study reassesses the observational and cosmological constraints on higher-dimensional PBHs in Randall--Sundrum cosmologies. Constraints from direct Hawking radiation, unresolved diffuse gamma-ray backgrounds, microlensing surveys, and energy injection into the cosmic microwave background are reanalysed in light of the modified higher-dimensional evaporation dynamics and updated observational surveys. Taken together, these results identify viable regions of parameter space in which PBHs can account for the entirety of dark matter while remaining consistent with current observational bounds. Notably, due to the enhanced accretion epoch, PBHs capable of constituting a significant fraction of dark matter may originate from masses below the effective four-dimensional Planck scale. This thesis thus puts forward a dark matter candidate with a distinct evolutionary history and observational signatures today.
title: Primordial black holes in braneworld gravity: A gateway to hidden dimensions and the dark Universe

abstract: Stacking is the standard route to signal-to-noise in cluster weak lensing, but it destroys the cluster-by-cluster information that scaling-relation studies need. We instead fit every cluster's individual $ΔΣ$ profile simultaneously, tying its mass and concentration to its own richness, redshift and magnitude gap, and compare with two stacked analyses of the same data: a forward-modelled stack sharing the same model and priors, and the standard two-step analysis. The magnitude gap (the BCG-to-brightest-satellite magnitude difference) enters the concentration, which the fossil-group picture ties to earlier assembly and more relaxed systems. On mock populations with triaxial haloes and miscentering, at DES Y3-like and LSST-like density, all three analyses recover the injected gap slope $γ_{\mathrm{cm}}$ with uncertainties that match the scatter between realisations, but not equally precisely: the joint fit scatters 1.2--1.3 times less than the forward-modelled stack, and 2 (DES-like) to 6.5 (LSST-like) times less than the two-step analysis, which is also biased in several other scaling-relation parameters. Applied to WaZP clusters with DES Y3 shears, the joint and forward-modelled fits agree on the gap coupling once the mass at fixed richness also depends on the gap, $γ_{\mathrm{cm}} = 0.065 \pm 0.033$ (forward-modelled) and$0.007^{+0.032}_{-0.033}$~mag$^{-1}$ (joint); the joint value is consistent with no coupling, so neither is a detection. The mass--concentration slope is consistent with zero in both, as expected from the upturn of the \citet{diemer2019} relation over this mass range. A gap coupling obtained in a model where the gap enters only the concentration need not survive a modest extension of that model.
comment: 31 pages, 24 figures, to be submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
title: Joint Fit of Galaxy Cluster Scaling Relations from Individual Weak Lensing Data: Comparison with Stacked Analysis and a Real Data Test

abstract: We investigate the impact of applying the uninformative Jeffreys prior in a re-analysis of DESI DR2 BAO, Planck 2018 CMB, and Type Ia Supernovae (DES-SN5YR, DES-Dovekie, Pantheon+, Union3). We incorporate this prior into new posterior inference and evidence calculations. We introduce novel techniques for interpreting the Jeffreys prior physically. To overcome the computational expense of the Jeffreys prior, we develop a fully $\texttt{JAX}$-based pipeline consisting of $\texttt{CosmoPower-JAX}$ emulators, gradient-based posterior inference using the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS), and evidence calculations using $\texttt{JAX}$-accelerated nested sampling. We demonstrate that while the parameter constraints on $w_0$ and $w_a$ remain robust to prior choice (exhibiting only minor shifts of the marginalised posterior towards the $\textit{Maximum A Posteriori}$ in less constraining dataset combinations), the Bayesian evidence is highly sensitive to the use of the Jeffreys prior; replacing uniform priors with the Jeffreys prior reverses the model-selection preference in dataset combinations that favour dynamical dark energy under the uniform prior, while strengthening existing preferences for $Λ$CDM. This is driven primarily by the significantly larger Occam penalty applied by the Jeffreys prior which penalises the overfitting of the data by a $w_0w_a$CDM model.
comment: 15 pages, to be submitted to OJA, code available at https://github.com/JoshL965/Jeffreys-prior-project
title: Exploring the Evidence for Evolving Dark Energy with the Jeffreys prior

abstract: Detailed UV-to-optical studies of galaxies at z >= 10 have largely focused on bright systems (MUV <= -20 mag), leaving intrinsically faint galaxies virtually unexplored to date. Combining NIRCam, NIRSpec, and MIRI imaging and spectroscopy, we investigate UNCOVER-ABELL2744-13151 (U13151), an ultra-faint galaxy at z = 9.7995 (MUV = -17.44 mag), magnified by Abell 2744 ($μ$ = 12.8). U13151 is very blue ($β$ ~ -2.64), ultra-low mass (log10(M*/Msun) ~ 6.68), young (~ 5.5 Myr), metal-poor (Z ~ 3-6% Zsun), and compact (Re ~ 122 pc). It exhibits negligible dust attenuation, extreme ionization conditions, and intense star formation (sSFR(Ha) ~ 94 Gyr-1, or equivalently M*/SFR(Ha) ~ 10.6 Myr). Despite similarities with much brighter galaxies, its low C/O, approximately solar Ne/O, and undetected nitrogen emission suggest enrichment dominated by core-collapse supernovae, in stark contrast with similar nitrogen-enhanced systems. U13151 might be undergoing its first major episode of star formation, assembling most (if not all) of its M* through five unresolved clumps. Its high ionizing photon production efficiency (log10($ξ_{\rm ion}$/ (Hz erg-1)) ~ 25.64) suggests, through a simple toy model, suggests, through a simple toy model, that similarly short-lived episodes could contribute significantly to the ionizing photon budget of low-mass galaxies during Cosmic Reionization. We explore different evolutionary scenarios, from U13151-like galaxies potentially representing the progenitors of Blue Monsters at higher redshifts to the possibility that such systems could be the early building blocks of present-day Milky Way-like galaxies. Our results highlight the fundamental role of MIRI in studying galaxies in the early Universe and the urgent need to investigate the faintest, lowest-mass systems to shed light on the fundamental physics driving the earliest phases of galaxy formation.
